episodes.212687: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through southern Middle Tennessee during the late afternoon of June 13, 2026. As these thunderstorms crossed the Tennessee River, they produced strong winds, downing a couple trees in the area. The thunderstorms weakened as they moved into a more unfavorable environment east of Interstate 65.
episodes.212689: A line of thunderstorms moved through southern Middle Tennessee during the early afternoon of June 14, 2026. These thunderstorms produced strong winds as they tracked east, particularly in Lawrence County where a few downed trees were reported.
episodes.212693: Very hot and humid conditions were in place as an upper level disturbance moved through.
episodes.212697: An approaching cold front and trough of low pressure combined with a very unstable airmass produced conditions conducive to robust thunderstorm development. An inland moving sea breeze aided in the development of a large cluster of thunderstorms stretching generally along the Highway 17 corridor from Onslow to Craven County, and then northeastward from there through Beaufort, western Hyde, and Tyrrell County. Several of these storms became severe, producing damaging wind gusts as high as around 70 mph. One storm produced up to quarter sized hail across central Tyrrell County.
episodes.212803: A cold front backed south and westward through eastern and central NM during the early morning hours of June 14th. Abundant low-level moisture pushed in behind this front, reaching the Continental Divide. This provided fuel for thunderstorm development during the early afternoon hours of the 14th with on such severe thunderstorm producing severe wind gusts in Rio Rancho. Afternoon thunderstorms developed again over the northern mountains and along the central mountain chain of NM June 15th. There were reports of 8 inch tree branches down in Taos landing over power lines from severe thunderstorm wind gusts. Other thunderstorms advanced eastward off the Sangre de Cristo Mountains organizing into a line producing severe wind gusts through northeastern NM. This line of storms over northeastern NM eventually advanced all the way through east-central NM and into the TX Panhandle. Severe wind gusts reaching 60 mph or more were observed in Guadalupe County, including at Santa Rosa Lake State Park.
episodes.212993: A line of storms developed during the afternoon of 6/14 along strong low level convergence associated with a prefrontal trough. Moderate instability with MLCAPE around 1500 J/kg and enhancement from an outflow boundary led to damaging wind gusts in a portion of the line.
episodes.213080: Scattered thunderstorms moved across portions of northeast Illinois during the late evening of June 13th into the early morning of June 14th, producing isolated wind damage.
episodes.213168: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Between 3 and 6 inches of rainfall fell with this system. Some fatalities occurred from the flooding.
episodes.213184: Severe thunderstorms with tornadoes and damaging winds occurred late in the evening of June 13, 2026. Repeated rounds of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding and river flooding. Rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches occurred with these rounds of storms.
episodes.213341: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
episodes.213342: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
episodes.213345: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms. One particularly intense cluster resulted in wind gusts estimated to 80 mph in Frederick County, Maryland.
episodes.213354: Increasing heat and humidity led to scattered strong to severe thunderstorms.
episodes.213703: A line of thunderstorms developed during the afternoon hours ahead of a cold front moving through the region.
episodes.213717: Scattered supercells developed and moved into north central Kansas in the late afternoon period. Hazards reported were initially large hail to 2 inches in diameter before the convection formed into a line, tracking southeast during the evening hours. The storms produced winds around 70 mph and heavy rainfall amounts to 3.5 inches.
episodes.213759: A cold front dropped south into the region and combined with a warm, moist and unstable airmass to bring isolated showers and thunderstorms to the region on the afternoon and evening of June 13. Storms primarily affected the east and northeast Texas Panhandle with damaging winds and small hail.
episodes.213810: An incoming cold front helped generate showers and thunderstorms across portions of west Texas and southeast New Mexico as it moved across the area throughout the day. Flash flooding was reported in Hobbs and in Culberson County due to heavy rain.
episodes.213811: An incoming cold front helped generate showers and thunderstorms across portions of west Texas and southeast New Mexico as it moved across the area throughout the day. Flash flooding was reported in Hobbs and in Culberson County due to heavy rain.
episodes.213894: A low pressure system stations across central Quebec with a trailing cold front across the Great Lakes allowed for central Pennsylvania to experience residence time within the warm sector throughout much of the day on June 14, 2026. Initial shower activity during the morning and early afternoon hours stayed largely non-hazardous before convection began across western Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours. Clearing skies after the initial showers and thunderstorms allowed for instability to rise above 1000 J/kg across much of the region by the late afternoon hours with effective bulk shear in the 40-50 knot range. Of note, 0-1km shear magnitudes across much of the region trended upwards of 30 knots, which allowed for ample low-level spin within thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening hours. As the cold front began to move eastward across central Pennsylvania, a line of thunderstorms pushed across the region with many kinks in the line exhibiting tornadic circulations. Ahead of the line, some thunderstorms began to form where clear skies allowed for destabilization with some cells exhibiting supercellular characteristics. Wind damage was first observed during the early evening hours, where multiple trees and wires were down across western Pennsylvania. Damage continued as thunderstorms moved further east throughout the evening hours. In terms of cells ahead of the line, wind damage was mostly concentrated across Franklin, York, and Lancaster Counties. Four tornadoes occurred with the storm system on June 14th; an EF-1 near Grand Valley in Warren County, an EF-0 near Homer Township in Potter County, an EF-1 near Pine Glen in Centre County, and an EF-1 near Kirkwood in Lancaster County. A microburst also occurred in York County, where widespread tree damage was observed near Brogue.
episodes.213982: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northeastern Oklahoma during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms that moved through Arkansas. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to two inches in diameter and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northeastern Oklahoma during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced a number of damaging wind reports.
episodes.213983: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the late afternoon of the 13th, along a pre-existing outflow boundary from earlier organized thunderstorms. The atmosphere became very unstable during the afternoon across the region, and deep layer wind shear was strong. This combination resulted in several supercell thunderstorms developing, which produced large hail up to quarter size and damaging wind gusts. ||Thunderstorms also developed along a cold front stretching across south central Kansas during the late afternoon and early evening. These thunderstorms moved southeast across northwest Arkansas during the evening and organized into a squall line, which produced damaging wind.
episodes.213999: Early summer southwesterly flow combined with the effects of the Atlantic Sea breeze resulted in numerous thunderstorms over northeast FL.
episodes.214000: On June 10th, an inverted trough over the Atlantic Ocean waters adjacent to the northeast Florida and southeast Georgia waters developed coastal showers that moved onshore in the overnight into morning hours. Showers interacted with the land breeze creating a convergent line of heavy showers that caused flooding along the coast. Moist west-southwest flow then developed resulting in typical summertime sea breeze thunderstorms each afternoon into evening for the next several days. The strongest storms were along the sea breeze collisions near HWY 301 and U.S. Route 23.
episodes.214038: An early season rain event led to some localized flash flooding across portions of northern Arizona.
episodes.214143: An approaching cold front and trough of low pressure combined with a very unstable airmass produced conditions conducive for scattered thunderstorm development. An inland moving sea breeze aided in the development of a cluster of thunderstorms with this activity tracking from the Coastal Plain of Eastern North Carolina east through the afternoon and early evening hours impacting portions of the Albemarle Sound and inland rivers. A few isolated strong to severe thunderstorms developed bringing a strong wind threat to portions of the Alligator River.
episodes.214198: A thunderstorm produced 1 inch hail in South Rockwood.
episodes.214203: Thunderstorms moving through western Lake Erie produced wind gusts to near 40 knots and a waterspout.
episodes.214347: Several rounds of severe thunderstorms impacted northern Oklahoma on the 13th and early morning hours of the 14th. The first featured a slowly decaying line of thunderstorms during the early morning of the 13th, producing a few observations of severe winds and wind damage. Later in the afternoon, a pair of supercell thunderstorms developed along a remnant outflow boundary across the region. Provided strong instability and steep lapse rates, several reports of large hail and damaging wind gusts were received with this activity. Later, a semi-organized convective line (along an approaching cold front) impacted similar areas, leading to additional reports of mainly damaging/severe wind gusts.
episodes.214365: A mid-level trough dragged a cold front through the Mid-Atlantic and brought scattered thunderstorms to the forecast area. Inverted V-profiles in the weather sounding and high DCAPE values (>1000 J/kg) supported conditions favorable for damaging wind gusts in the form of wet microbursts with these storms. Severe weather potential was limited due to lackluster dew points and absence of wind shear. Nevertheless, several trees were reported down with almost half of them in Buckingham County.
episodes.214655: A typical summertime pattern produced scattered afternoon showers and thunderstorms with isolated severe weather reported.
episodes.214693: A strong line of thunderstorms swept across West Virginia on the afternoon of June 14th ahead of a cold front. The environment that day was conducive for storms to thrive, and reached strengths that caused a swath of tree and power line damage from the Ohio River to the Appalachian Mountains. The line of storms continued to steadily shift eastward with the arrival of the cold front that evening, with the risk of damaging wind gusts also coming to an end.
episodes.214697: As a line of strong thunderstorms began to develop on the afternoon of June 14th, a few sub-severe gusts were observed in southeast Ohio. This resulted in a tree to blow down in Lawrence County before gaining strength as storms progressed out of the state and east of the Ohio River.
episodes.214759: Isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms developed along a quasi-stationary front extending across southern Missouri and northwest Tennessee during the afternoon hours of June 13, 2026.  These storms were supported by SBCAPE values of 3000 to 4000 J/kg and 0-6km bulk shear values of around 30 knots. The storms formed into a line by late afternoon, with several reports of damaging winds. Slow-moving storms combined with precipitable water values around 2 inches to produce heavy rainfall and isolated flash flooding.
episodes.214899: A line of severe storms rapidly developed along an advancing cold front across central Kansas during the evening hours of June 13. At the same time, a left-moving supercell developed in Sumner County and quickly moved northeastward into the Flint Hills. Storms eventually merged and became a large complex of strong to severe storms that moved through south-central and southeast Kansas during the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 85 mph winds and up to softball size hail.
episodes.214993: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northern Ohio. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northeast Ohio, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters.  At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
episodes.214996: A line of thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front Sunday afternoon and moved southeast across Lake Erie into portions of Northwest Pennsylvania. Storms became strong to severe as they moved southeast over the Lake Erie Islands and towards the lakeshore, bringing damaging wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph. Storms continued to intensify as they continued east to southeast into Northwest Pennsylvania, resulting in peak wind gusts in excess of 70 mph at times and hail slightly larger than quarters, particularly near the OH/PA border across Northwest Pennsylvania where a few tornadoes also occurred. At the height of the event, over 150,000 power outages were reported across Ohio and Northwest Pennsylvania.
episodes.215138: A stalled frontal boundary over eastern North Carolina and southern Virginia interacted with an upper-level system to produce isolated severe storms across Sampson, Halifax, Nash, Guilford, and Johnston Counties.
episodes.215148: Cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through southwest North Carolina in a marginally supportive environment during the evening hours, producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215149: Cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms moved through southeast Tennessee in a marginally supportive environment during the early evening hours, producing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.215312: Scattered thunderstorms moved into upstate South Carolina from Georgia during the early afternoon. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Pickens County.
episodes.215442: Aided by a cold front and a shortwave, a strong line of thunderstorms developed in central Ohio and quickly progressed east across western Pennsylvania and northern West Virginia. A moisture rich environment with mid to upper 60s dew points and mid 70s temperatures supported a favorable setup with MLCAPE values around 1000 J/kg and strong effective shear of 40-50 knots. Widespread swaths of wind damage were noted with 60-80 mph wind, and plenty of low level shear also supported embedded mesovortices and transient tornadoes within the line of thunderstorms.

A National Weather Service storm Survey determined that a broad area of damaging straight-line winds impacted portions of Jasper and northern Newton Counties. Damage began in the Joplin and Webb City areas and continued to the east and northeast through the I-49 Corridor from Diamond to Carthage before winds weakened. Winds from 75 to 95 mph uprooted or snapped numerous trees and downed large limbs. Several trees were down on homes. Multiple power lines and poles were down in the impacted area. A near 9 mile wide swath of significant damaging winds of 85 to 95 mph damaged multiple buildings, causing significant structural damage to a few. Several outbuildings were picked up or rolled to the east and several vehicles had trees or large limbs on them.

The National Weather Service storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado with peak winds of 90mph touched down 1 mile east southeast of Fidelity. The tornado lifted and rolled a secured carport before moving to the east northeast. Multiple trees were were uprooted or snapped off between 4 and 6 feet up along an intermittent path to a home along County Road 120. There were multiple 2 to 3 foot in diameter trees downed in a convergent pattern, with a home suffering significant roof and structural damage from the fallen tree. In addition, a truck was crushed under the a tree before the tornado lifted just east of the home in an open field.

A brief tornado touched down along Highway 97 to the south of Capps Creek. The intermittent tornado path tracked to the east-northeast before lifting just west of Highway 37, between Monett and Purdy. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Walls collapsed on two farm outbuildings, with sheet metal tossed over 300 yards.

A tornado began near Farm Road 1078, just to the northwest of Butterfield. NWS ground surveys concluded that the tornado path tracked to the east across Highway 37. A couple of old wooden power poles snapped or were brought down along Highway 37. Several uprooted trees and large branches snapped along the path. Sentinel 2 satellite data analysis revealed that the tornado continued to the northeast, crossing State Highway U, producing an intermittent path of tree damage about 6.6 miles long. Satellite data revealed the tornado was 350 yards at its widest point with estimated max winds of 85 mph.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief EF-0 tornado touched down on the west side of Conneautville, Pennsylvania, at about 4:10 PM EDT on Sunday, June 14, 2026. The tornado left a path of damage, uprooting several trees and snapping large limbs along Mulberry Lane and Mulberry Street. The circulation then moved east across Mulberry Street, causing additional tree damage before dissipating shortly thereafter. Additionally, several trees were uprooted and snapped along State Highway 198. Based on the observed damage, the tornado's maximum winds were estimated at 85 mph, yielding an EF-0 rating. The tornado was 100 yards wide. It was brief and produced a relatively short damage path before evolving into straight-line thunderstorm winds. Although the tornadic circulation ended, strong straight-line winds persisted south of the tornado path. These winds caused additional damage, including several trees downed across the railroad tracks near Main Street and Smith Avenue. Maximum straight-line wind speeds reached 80 mph.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief EF-1 tornado touched down in central Crawford County at approximately 4:28 PM EDT, south of Dibble Hill Road and east of Theuret Hill Road, and tracked southeast. The tornado snapped several large tree limbs near the point of touchdown before crossing Stoltz Road, where several large trees were uprooted and fell onto a detached garage. A power pole snapped and fell toward the northwest even as the tornado moved southeast. Leaves and hay debris were scattered and pasted across the east side of a barn and nearby structures, indicating rotational winds. Additional trees were snapped and uprooted south of the property and within a tree line to the east. Based on the damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, yielding an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 75 yards. The National Weather Service Cleveland thanks the Crawford County EMA for its assistance during the storm survey.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that a brief tornado touched down in central Crawford County near Leimbach Road at approximately 4:29 PM EDT. The tornado touched down west of Leimbach Road and north of Double Hill Road, then moved generally east-southeast. Damage consisted primarily of snapped and uprooted trees. Several trees were snapped near the point of touchdown, and a falling tree clipped and damaged a well-constructed detached garage. As the tornado crossed Leimbach Road, several large hardwood trees were uprooted. The fallen trees were oriented toward the northeast, consistent with the localized tornadic wind field despite the tornado's overall east-southeast movement. Based on the observed damage, maximum wind speeds were estimated at 95 mph, yielding an EF-1 tornado rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards and produced a short, intermittent damage path before dissipating.

A National Weather Service Cleveland storm survey determined that an EF-1 tornado touched down at approximately 4:51 PM EDT on Sunday, June 14, 2026, along Lippert Road, just east of the intersection with Mallory Road in Crawford County. The tornado tracked east along Lippert Road, causing significant damage to one residence, including roof damage, the loss of an attached porch, damage to four vehicles, displacement of an RV approximately 50 feet, and damage to a garage roof. An additional six homes sustained minor damage, including damage to roofs, siding, and windows. As the tornado continued east, numerous trees were blown down, blocking driveways and roadways. Several large limbs snapped and fell onto a barn and a nearby home. The tornado gradually weakened and dissipated northwest of the intersection of Lippert Road and Vincent Road. Based on the observed damage, maximum winds were estimated at 90 mph, resulting in an EF-1 rating. The tornado had an estimated maximum width of 50 yards. The National Weather Service Cleveland appreciates the assistance provided for this storm survey and thanks Crawford County EMA for their support in documenting the damage.
